items.title: If a stock falls 50% then rises 50%, you've LOST money
items.claim: Stock at 100. Falls 50%: now 50. Rises 50%: now 75. Two equal-percentage moves in opposite directions don't cancel.

options.text: Percentages are RATIOS, not amounts. The 50% drop reduces the base; the subsequent 50% rise is on a smaller base. To recover from a -50% loss you need a +100% gain

items.reveal:
To go from x to y, percentage change is (y - x) / x.

Loss of L percent: new value = old * (1 - L/100).
Gain of G percent: new value = old * (1 + G/100).

For symmetric percent moves NOT to cancel, multiply: (1 - 0.5)(1 + 0.5) = 0.75. Always less than 1 if the magnitude is the same.

Recovery table:
- Lose 10%: need 11.1% to recover.
- Lose 25%: need 33.3% to recover.
- Lose 50%: need 100% to recover.
- Lose 75%: need 300% to recover.
- Lose 90%: need 900% to recover.

Applications:
- Drawdowns in investing: deep losses require enormous gains to recover. A 50% bear market loss takes years of strong returns to break even.
- Discounted prices then surcharged: 50% off followed by 50% on actually leaves you at 75% of original price (consumer gets a deal).
- Inflation: 10% inflation for 7 years halves purchasing power, even though 70% < 100%.

Geometric vs arithmetic mean: a stock returning +50%, -50%, +50%, -50% has arithmetic mean return 0% but geometric (actual) mean of ((1.5 * 0.5 * 1.5 * 0.5)^0.25 - 1) = -13.4%/period.
items.why: Percentages feel symmetric. They're multiplicative ratios that don't cancel directly. Anyone interpreting investment returns, weight changes, price comparisons or compound growth without realising this misreads the data.

items.title: Two equal pours of wine and water never separate again
items.claim: Pour a cup of wine into a barrel of water. Stir. Now pour a cup of the mixture back into the wine. Compared to the original: is there more wine in the water-barrel, or more water in the wine-barrel?

options.text: More wine in water (because it was poured first)
More water in wine (because the second cup contained mixture, not pure water)
Equal — by conservation of volume, the amount of wine missing from the wine barrel exactly equals the amount of water now in the wine barrel
Cannot be determined without more information

items.reveal:
Both barrels started with their own volume (V wine and V water). After two exchanges of one cup each, the volumes are still V wine and V water (volume is conserved in each barrel).

Let's say the wine barrel now contains x amount of water and (V - x) wine. The wine barrel's contents totals V — so by mass balance, V - (V - x) = x amount of wine has LEFT the wine barrel. Where did it go? It is now in the water barrel.

So: water in wine barrel = x; wine in water barrel = x. Always equal — regardless of how messy the mixing was, or whether the cups were exact, or how much you stirred.

This is a classic riddle dating to mediaeval mathematics. People reach for arithmetic and get tangled in fractions. A two-line conservation argument settles it without computation.

Generalisation: for ANY pair of equal-volume transfers (cup A to barrel B, then equal-volume cup B' to barrel A), the impurity in each ends up equal. The riddle is independent of mixing details.

Lesson for problem-solving: pure-conservation arguments often resolve mixing problems faster than direct calculation. The same idea underlies many chemistry-stoichiometry problems and the 'rule of alligation' in pharmacy.
items.why: Mixing problems feel like they need detailed arithmetic. Conservation reasoning bypasses the arithmetic entirely — and is more reliable, because it's robust to the details you don't know.

items.title: Compound interest of 7% turns 100 into 14,974 over 75 years
items.claim: Simple interest at 7% for 75 years: 100 + (75 x 7) = 625. Compound interest at 7% for 75 years: 100 x 1.07^75 = 14,974. The same rate, the same time. Compounding multiplies the result by 24x.
items.prompt: Why does compound interest diverge so dramatically?

options.text: Compound interest grows exponentially (multiplicatively each period); simple interest grows linearly (additively). Over long horizons, exponential growth always vastly exceeds linear, no matter the rate
The two are basically the same after enough time
Compound interest only works for whole-year periods

items.reveal_title: The rule of 72 and the magic of compounding
items.reveal:
Compound interest: each period, interest is paid on (principal + accumulated interest). Mathematically: A = P (1 + r)^n.
Simple interest: A = P (1 + r * n).

Rule of 72: at compound rate r% per year, money doubles in about 72/r years. At 7%, doubling time ~10.3 years. In 75 years that's ~7 doublings, so ~128x the original.

Applied historically: Einstein supposedly called compound interest 'the eighth wonder of the world' (apocryphal but illustrative). It explains:
- Why starting to save in your 20s vs your 40s makes such a huge difference.
- Why credit card debt at 20% APR explodes if minimum payments are made.
- Why long-run stock returns (averaging ~7% real) translate into vast wealth over careers.

For short horizons (1-2 periods), compound and simple interest are nearly equal. For long horizons, the gap is enormous. The gap is the 'magic' that financial planners try to communicate to young people, often unsuccessfully.

Negative compounding (decay) works the same way: 7% inflation halves purchasing power in ~10 years.
items.why: Linear and exponential are taught as adjacent concepts. They diverge in practice so dramatically that human intuition completely fails for long horizons. Anyone making long-term financial decisions needs to feel this in their bones.
